title: In Mrs Dorling's living-room
body: On her second visit the narrator is let in by a girl of about fifteen and shown into the living-room. She stops, horrified: she is in a room she knows and does not know, among things she did want to see again but which oppress her in the strange atmosphere, the tasteless arrangement, the ugly furniture and the muggy smell. She sits down and rubs the woollen table-cloth, following the lines of its pattern and looking for a burn mark on the edge that had never been repaired. The girl pours tea from a white pot with a gold border on the lid and takes spoons from a box that her mother says is antique. Over the tea-table hangs a still life; as a child the narrator had always fancied the apple on the pewter plate. The girl says they use everything and once even ate off the plates on the wall, though it was nothing special. (Passage summarised from the chapter for practice.)
